title: Grade 4 ENGLISH LANGUAGE — 11.3.1 Grammar in Use: Language Patterns (Interrogatives)

PAGE 1: Overview

OVERVIEW
========

Interrogatives are words we use to ask questions. In this sub-strand you will find who, what, where, when and whose in texts about sport, build questions with them, and answer those questions clearly. Asking well helps you learn rules, find lost kit and talk about your favourite game.

## Strand 11.0: Sports: My Favourite Game
Sub-strand 11.3.1: Grammar in Use: Language Patterns (Interrogatives)
Suggested lessons: 3

## Learning outcomes
By the end of the sub-strand, the learner should be able to:
a) identify interrogatives in a variety of texts for communication clarity
b) use interrogatives in a variety of contexts for effective communication
c) respond to a variety of questions based on interrogatives for effective communication
d) realise the importance of interrogatives in communication

## What this sub-strand covers
• Interrogatives

## Key inquiry questions
1. Why do we ask questions?
2. Which words do we use to ask questions?

## Core competencies
• Learning to Learn: This is enhanced as the learner uses appropriate interrogatives to ask questions.
• Digital Literacy: The learner interacts with digital devices to watch videos and type sentences.

## Values
• Unity: The learner collaborates with peers to perform task such as watching videos and typing sentences on a digital device.
• Respect: This is promoted as the learner is able to accommodate the views of others during the discussion.

## Pertinent and contemporary issues
• Self-esteem: This is built in the learner as they ask and answer questions using interrogatives about their favourite sports making them discover their talents.

## Links to other learning areas
• The learner can relate the concept of interrogatives to question and answer sessions in Religious Education among other learning areas.

## Source

PAGE 2: Lesson 1: Spotting who, what, where, when and whose

LESSON 1: SPOTTING WHO, WHAT, WHERE, WHEN AND WHOSE
===================================================

## What you will learn
• Name five interrogatives and the kind of answer each one seeks.
• Find them in questions about sport.
• Explain why questions matter in communication.

Curriculum outcomes: a) identify interrogatives in a variety of texts for communication clarity; d) realise the importance of interrogatives in communication

## Introduction
A teammate says, 'The match is ready.' You still do not know the place or the time. One well-chosen question fills the gap. The first word of that question tells everyone what kind of answer you need.

## Notes
### Five interrogatives
An interrogative is a question word. In this sub-strand we use five:

- who asks about a person
- what asks about a thing, an idea or an action
- where asks about a place
- when asks about a time
- whose asks about an owner

Look at these questions from a games lesson.

Who is the captain? (a person)
What is in the kit bag? (a thing)
Where is the field? (a place)
When does the race start? (a time)
Whose whistle is on the desk? (an owner)

Each question ends with a question mark. The interrogative usually comes first.

### Find them in a short text
Our coach asked us five questions before the match. Who will lead the team? What must we carry? Where shall we meet? When will the referee blow the whistle? Whose name is first on the list? We could not start until those answers were clear.

If you cover the question word, the rest of the sentence no longer tells you what is being asked. That is how you test that the word is doing the work.

### Why we ask
Questions help us learn, check a fact and include other people. A player who asks when the practice is will not arrive late. A player who asks whose bottle this is will not take the wrong one. A class that can ask clear questions understands the game more quickly. Interrogatives make those questions precise, so the answer can be precise too.

## Key words
• interrogative — a word used to ask a question, such as who, what, where, when or whose
• question mark — the sign ? that comes at the end of a question
• owner — the person something belongs to

## Worked examples

### Example 1
Name the interrogative and say what it asks for: Where do we practise on Friday?

Working:
1. The question word is at the beginning.
2. Where always asks for a place.

Answer: Where. It asks for a place.

### Example 2
Which interrogative fits? ______ shoes are under the bench?

Working:
1. The question is about an owner, not a place or a time.
2. Whose asks about an owner.

Answer: Whose

## Activity: Mark the question words
You will need: A newspaper, magazine, brochure or textbook page, A pencil
1. In pairs, read a short sports report, a school notice or a page your teacher provides.
2. Underline every who, what, where, when and whose you find.
3. Beside each one, write person, thing, place, time or owner.
4. If the page has no questions, turn three statements into questions and mark the new interrogatives.

## Practice
1. Match each word to what it asks: who, where, when, whose.
2. Underline the interrogative: What did the coach say about fair play?
3. Why do we ask questions?
4. Which interrogative is missing? ______ is the captain of the netball team?

## Summary
• Who, what, where, when and whose are interrogatives.
• Each one asks for a different kind of answer.
• A question mark ends the question.

### Answers to practice
1. who — a person; where — a place; when — a time; whose — an owner.
2. What
3. To learn, to check facts and to get a precise answer so we can act or understand.
4. Who

PAGE 3: Lesson 2: Building questions

LESSON 2: BUILDING QUESTIONS
============================

## What you will learn
• Form questions with who, what, where, when and whose.
• Use the right word order.
• Ask a partner about a game or a picture.

Curriculum outcomes: b) use interrogatives in a variety of contexts for effective communication

## Introduction
Knowing the five words is only the start. A question has an order. 'Where the field is?' is not yet a finished question. 'Where is the field?' is.

## Notes
### Word order
Many questions follow this pattern:

interrogative + helping verb + subject + rest + ?

Where do you practise?
When does the match start?
What did the captain say?

Who and what can be the subject. Then you do not add do or does:

Who leads the team?
What happened after the whistle?

Whose comes before the thing owned:

Whose kit is this?
Whose name did the coach call?

### Choose the word that matches the gap
Start from the answer and work backwards.

- Answer: Amina. Question: Who scored the last goal?
- Answer: A red ball. Question: What is in the bag?
- Answer: On the field. Question: Where is the match?
- Answer: At four o'clock. Question: When do we meet?
- Answer: The referee's. Question: Whose whistle is on the table?

If the answer is a person, do not begin with where. If the answer is a time, do not begin with whose.

### From a picture or a video
Look at a picture of a game and ask only what you cannot be sure of, or what you want a partner to notice. 'Who is holding the ball?' 'What is the goalkeeper doing?' 'Where is the coach standing?' Keep your voice friendly. A question is not a trap.

Write the questions in your book or type them. Start each one with a capital letter and end with a question mark.

## Key words
• helping verb — a verb such as is, are, do, does or did that helps to make a question
• word order — the order of words in a sentence
• subject — the person or thing the sentence is about

## Worked examples

### Example 1
Make a question whose answer is 'Behind the stadium'.

Working:
1. The answer is a place.
2. Begin with where, then the helping verb.

Answer: Where is the team?

### Example 2
Correct this question: Whose is bottle this?

Working:
1. Whose comes directly before the noun.
2. The pattern is Whose + noun + verb.

Answer: Whose bottle is this?

## Activity: Questions from a picture
You will need: A picture, cartoon or short video of a game, Exercise books or a shared word processor
1. View the picture or video together.
2. Each learner writes five questions, one beginning with who, what, where, when and whose.
3. Ask a partner your questions. The partner answers in words, not only by pointing.
4. Type two correct questions, or copy them neatly, and swap books to check capital letters and question marks.

## Practice
1. Write a where question about a football field.
2. Write a when question about athletics practice.
3. Correct the order: What the captain did say?
4. Write a whose question about a kit bag.

## Summary
• Begin with the interrogative that matches the answer you want.
• Use helping verbs such as do, does and did when the pattern needs them.
• Whose sits directly before the thing that is owned.

### Answers to practice
1. Example: Where is the football field?
2. Example: When does athletics practice begin?
3. What did the captain say?
4. Example: Whose kit bag is under the bench?

PAGE 4: Lesson 3: Answering questions fully

LESSON 3: ANSWERING QUESTIONS FULLY
===================================

## What you will learn
• Give an answer that matches the interrogative.
• Answer in a sentence when the situation needs it.
• Notice when an answer does not fit the question.

Curriculum outcomes: c) respond to a variety of questions based on interrogatives for effective communication; d) realise the importance of interrogatives in communication

## Introduction
If someone asks when the race starts and you answer 'On the field', you have named a place. The listener is still late. A useful answer matches the question word.

## Notes
### Match the answer to the word
Listen to the interrogative before you speak.

- Who? Name a person: The captain is Hassan.
- What? Name a thing or an action: We need a ball and a whistle.
- Where? Name a place: We meet on the school field.
- When? Name a time: The match starts at four o'clock.
- Whose? Name an owner: It is the referee's whistle.

A one-word answer can be enough among friends: 'Where is my bottle?' 'Here.' In class, and whenever the listener may not see what you see, answer in a full sentence. 'Your bottle is under the bench.'

### A question-and-answer game
Coach: Who will keep the score?
Asha: I will keep the score.
Coach: What must the players leave at the side?
Juma: They must leave their bags at the side.
Coach: Where is the first-aid box?
Asha: The first-aid box is in the office.
Coach: When do we stop for water?
Juma: We stop for water at half-time.
Coach: Whose turn is it to carry the ball?
Asha: It is my turn.

Each answer uses information from the question. Nobody answers a when question with a person's name.

### If you do not know
It is honest to say, 'I do not know yet.' Then ask someone who does, or look at the notice. Inventing a time or an owner causes confusion. You can also ask for the question to be repeated: 'Could you say the question again, please?'

### Why careful answers matter
Sport depends on shared information. The right person, object, place, time and owner keep a match fair and safe. The same skill helps in every subject: read the question word, then give the kind of fact it asks for.

## Key words
• full sentence — a sentence with a subject and a verb that can stand alone
• half-time — the short break in the middle of a match
• first-aid box — a box of simple supplies for treating small injuries

## Worked examples

### Example 1
The question is 'When is the competition?' Which answer fits: 'Tomorrow morning' or 'The captain'?

Working:
1. When asks for a time.
2. A person's name does not tell the time.

Answer: Tomorrow morning.

### Example 2
Turn this short answer into a full sentence. Question: Whose shoes are these? Answer: Amina's.

Working:
1. Repeat the idea of the question.
2. Include the owner.

Answer: These shoes are Amina's. or They are Amina's shoes.

## Activity: Ask and answer in pairs
You will need: Question cards for who, what, where, when and whose, Exercise books
1. Write one sports question for each interrogative on a card.
2. Swap cards with a partner and answer in full sentences.
3. Check that the answer matches the question word. If it does not, ask the question again.
4. Choose your best pair of question and answer and read them to the class.

## Practice
1. Answer in a full sentence: Where do the players warm up?
2. A learner answers 'A ball' to the question 'Who is the referee?' What is wrong?
3. Answer: When should you drink water during a match?
4. Why should an answer match the interrogative?

## Summary
• Who needs a person, what a thing, where a place, when a time and whose an owner.
• Use a full sentence when a short answer would be unclear.
• Say you do not know rather than inventing a fact.

### Answers to practice
1. Example: The players warm up on the field.
2. Who asks for a person, but 'a ball' is a thing.
3. Example: You should drink water at half-time or when the coach allows a break.
4. So the listener gets the kind of fact they asked for and can act on it.
pages.quiz:
REVISION QUIZ — 11.3.1 GRAMMAR IN USE: LANGUAGE PATTERNS (INTERROGATIVES)
========================================

Answer all the questions, then mark yourself on the Answers tab.

1. Which word is an interrogative?
   A. quickly
   B. whose
   C. under
   D. and

2. Who asks about
   A. a place
   B. a person
   C. a time
   D. an owner only

3. When asks about
   A. a time
   B. a thing
   C. a colour
   D. a place

4. Choose the correct question.
   A. Whose bottle is this?
   B. Whose is bottle this?
   C. Whose this is bottle?
   D. Bottle whose this?

5. Which question asks for a place?
   A. Who scored?
   B. What is the score?
   C. Where is the field?
   D. When is half-time?

6. Correct the word order of: What the coach did say?
   A. What did the coach say?
   B. What say the coach did?
   C. Did what the coach say?
   D. Coach what did say the?

7. The question is 'Who blew the whistle?' A matching answer is
   A. At noon
   B. On the field
   C. The referee
   D. A red kit

8. The question is 'When does practice start?' A matching answer is
   A. After lunch
   B. The captain
   C. In the bag
   D. Neema's

9. Why are interrogatives important?

10. You do not know whose kit is on the bench. What is the best reply?
   A. Invent a name
   B. Say you do not know and ask the coach
   C. Hide the kit
   D. Answer with a place
pages.answers:
ANSWERS — 11.3.1 GRAMMAR IN USE: LANGUAGE PATTERNS (INTERROGATIVES)
========================================

1. B. whose
   Whose is a question word. The others are not interrogatives.

2. B. a person
   Who asks about a person.

3. A. a time
   When asks about time.

4. A. Whose bottle is this?
   Whose comes before the noun: Whose bottle is this?

5. C. Where is the field?
   Where asks for a place.

6. A. What did the coach say?
   What + did + subject + main verb.

7. C. The referee
   Who needs a person. The referee is a person.

8. A. After lunch
   After lunch tells the time. The other answers do not.

9. They make questions precise so we can learn, check facts and get the right kind of answer.
   The question word tells everyone what kind of information is needed.

10. B. Say you do not know and ask the coach
   It is honest to admit you do not know and then find out.

questions.explanation: It is honest to admit you do not know and then find out.
